editorial_contributions.text: Complete characterizations of compact sets with positive reach (i.e., proximally \(C^1\) sets) in the plane and of one-dimensional sets with positive reach in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) are provided, after the literature in the field is thoroughly reviewed. Then, the sets of positive reach in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) are investigated and the authors show, for instance, that the boundaries of such sets can be locally covered by finitely many semiconcave hypersurfaces, a corresponding result being provided also when the dimensions of the sets in discussion lies between \(0\) and \(d\). Earlier results from the literature are improved or corrected, too, while some of the newly shown statements are illustrated by examples.

title.title: On the structure of sets with positive reach

editorial_contributions.text:
The definition of a set with positive reach employs a familiar property of convex sets. Namely, a set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\) is said to have positive reach if, for some \(\varepsilon>0\), every point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}\left(x,A\right)<\varepsilon\) has
a nearest point \(a\in A\); that is, 
\[
\left\vert x-a\right\vert =\operatorname{dist}\left(  x,A\right)  .
\]
In [Math. Nachr. 297, No. 3, 932--942 (2024; Zbl 1536.53083)], \textit{A. Lytchak} described the local structure of \(k\)-dimensional sets with positive reach  in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), where \(k\leq d\), at points where the tangent cone of \(A\) is \(k\)-dimensional. The authors' main result provides a complete characterization of the local structure of two-dimensional sets \(A\) in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) with positive reach for \(d\geq3\). The proof uses Lytchak's results from [loc. cit.] and the authors' previous results. As a corollary, the authors prove that for every two-dimensional set with positive reach \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\), \(d\geq3\), and every \(a\in A\), there exists a compact set \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{2}\) with positive reach and \(0\in B\), together with a bi-Lipschitz mapping \(\psi:B\rightarrow A^{\ast}\), where \(A^{\ast}\) is a neighborhood of \(a\) in \(A\).

This corollary gives a positive answers to Question 1.7 in [loc. cit.].
